label: Ratio and regression estimators — mastery test (unseen)

items.stem: The ratio estimator of the population mean is:
items.explanation: The ratio estimator scales the sample mean by the known-to-sample auxiliary mean ratio.

items.stem: The regression estimator of the population mean is:
items.explanation: The regression estimator adds the fitted slope times the auxiliary mean discrepancy.

items.stem: Which relationship most naturally supports ratio estimation?
options: A constant y unrelated to x
A proportional relationship passing approximately through the origin
items.explanation: Ratio estimation is most plausible when y is approximately proportional to x.

items.stem: In ratio estimation, X̄ denotes:
options: The population auxiliary mean, usually known
items.explanation: X̄ is the known population auxiliary mean used as a benchmark.

items.stem: If X̄=x̄, the ratio estimator equals:
items.explanation: The adjustment factor X̄/x̄ is one, so the estimate reduces to ȳ.

items.stem: Which adjustment is used by the regression estimator?
items.explanation: Regression uses an additive slope-times-difference correction.

items.stem: ȳ=12, x̄=3, X̄=4. Find the ratio estimate.
items.explanation: 12×(4/3)=16. The calculation follows the stated sampling formula; identify the relevant population and sample quantities before interpreting the result.
items.check: The ratio factor is 4/3, so the adjusted mean is 16.

items.stem: ȳ=20, x̄=5, X̄=6 and b=2. Find the regression estimate.
items.explanation: 20+2(6−5)=22. The calculation follows the stated sampling formula; identify the relevant population and sample quantities before interpreting the result.
items.check: The auxiliary discrepancy is one and the slope adjustment is two.

items.stem: Which statement about the ratio estimator is correct?
options: It is generally biased in finite samples
It is identical to the regression estimator for every sample
items.explanation: A ratio of random sample quantities is generally not exactly design-unbiased.

items.stem: The first-order approximate variance of a ratio estimator under SRSWOR is based on:
items.explanation: The ratio residual captures variation left after proportional adjustment.

items.stem: ȳ=30, x̄=6, X̄=8. Find the ratio estimate.
items.explanation: 30×(8/6)=40. The calculation follows the stated sampling formula; identify the relevant population and sample quantities before interpreting the result.

items.stem: Which statements about ratio and regression estimation are true?
items.explanation: A, B and D are true; ratio estimation is not generally exactly unbiased.
statements: Ratio estimation uses X̄/x̄ as a multiplier.
The ratio estimator is exactly unbiased for every finite population.
Both use auxiliary information about x.

A.why: The ratio estimator multiplies the sample mean by X̄/x̄.

B.why: This is the additive regression adjustment.

C.why: The nonlinear ratio estimator is generally biased in finite samples.

D.why: Both methods use the auxiliary population mean.

items.stem: When may regression estimation be preferred over ratio estimation?
options: When x and y have no association
When the relationship is approximately linear but has a nonzero intercept
When sample x̄ is always equal to X̄
items.explanation: Regression allows a nonzero intercept, whereas ratio estimation imposes proportional scaling.

items.stem: ȳ=50, x̄=10, X̄=12 and b=1.5. Find the regression estimate.
items.explanation: 50+1.5(2)=53. The calculation follows the stated sampling formula; identify the relevant population and sample quantities before interpreting the result.
items.check: The auxiliary mean difference is two, producing an adjustment of three.

items.stem: Under SRSWOR, the first-order approximate ratio variance is:
items.explanation: The ratio residual variance, with the finite-population correction, drives the first-order approximation.

items.stem: Which statements about estimator properties are correct?
items.explanation: A, B and C are correct; an informative auxiliary variable does not guarantee improvement in every realised sample.
statements: Ratio estimation can have finite-sample bias.
A strong auxiliary relationship can reduce variance.
The regression adjustment is based on X̄−x̄.
Using auxiliary information guarantees a lower realised error for every sample.

A.why: The ratio estimator is generally biased in finite samples.

B.why: A strong relationship can reduce residual variation.

C.why: This difference is multiplied by the fitted slope.

D.why: Precision gains are design and population dependent, not guaranteed for every realised sample.

items.stem: ȳ=18, x̄=6, X̄=9. Find the ratio estimate.
items.explanation: 18×(9/6)=27. The calculation follows the stated sampling formula; identify the relevant population and sample quantities before interpreting the result.

items.stem: If X̄ is below x̄, the ratio adjustment (for positive means) will:
items.explanation: When X̄/x̄ is below one, the ratio estimator scales ȳ downward.

items.stem: For the regression estimator, if X̄=x̄, then:
options: The adjustment is zero and the estimate is ȳ
items.explanation: The additive adjustment b(X̄−x̄) is zero.

items.stem: ȳ=40, x̄=8, X̄=10. Find the ratio adjustment factor.
items.explanation: 10/8=1.25. The calculation follows the stated sampling formula; identify the relevant population and sample quantities before interpreting the result.
items.check: Divide the known population mean by the sample auxiliary mean.
